questions.question: In stochastic operations research, which description of a queueing system is correct?
options: Items are produced or ordered in advance and kept in stock until demand arrives to take them.
Jobs arrive at fixed known times and each one is served at once, so no job ever has to wait.
Jobs arrive over time, wait while the service capacity is occupied, are served and then leave.
A fixed set of jobs present at time $0$ is served one by one, and no new jobs arrive later.

questions.question: In an inventory system, items are stored until demand takes them. What can happen to a demand that finds no item in stock?
options: It is always lost, because a demand for an item cannot wait for the next replenishment.
It is either lost or it waits until a replenishment brings a new item into stock.
It always waits, because an inventory system backlogs every demand that cannot be met.
It is recorded as scrapped stock, in the same way as an item that passed its shelf life.

questions.question: For a single-server queue with $L(t)$ jobs in the system at time $t$, what does the time-average state probability $p(0)$ measure?
options: The long-run fraction of time that the system is empty, so the fraction of time the server is idle.
The long-run fraction of arriving jobs that find the system empty when they enter it.
The long-run fraction of time that the server is busy with at least one job in the system.
The probability that the system is empty at time $0$, when observation of $L(t)$ starts.

questions.question: A restaurant manager wants to know which fraction of the customers who want a hamburger leave without one because the shelf is empty. Which inventory performance measure is this?
options: The fraction of items scrapped, because those hamburgers were never sold to anyone.
The average time that hamburgers spend on the shelf before a customer buys them.
The fraction of time that the shelf is empty during the hours the restaurant is open.
The fraction of lost sales, the part of demand that could not be served from stock.

questions.question: Hamburgers on a restaurant shelf can be viewed as jobs waiting in a queue. In this view, which event plays the role of a hamburger's service completion?
options: The preparation of the batch of hamburgers when they are put on the shelf at minute $0$.
The scrapping of the hamburger when its selling time ends and it is taken off the shelf.
The arrival of the next customer who buys a hamburger and takes it off the shelf.
The moment the cashier finishes serving a customer who is waiting at the counter.

questions.question: A clinic follows $600$ patients who each visit $3$ times a year; a working year has $240$ working days and every consultation takes $12$ minutes. How many minutes of consultation work arise on an average working day?
options: $90$ minutes
$30$ minutes
$59.2$ minutes
$10$ minutes

questions.question: A restaurant puts $4$ hamburgers on the shelf at minute $0$; each can be sold for $10$ minutes. Customers who each buy one arrive at minutes $1$, $3$, $6$ and $9$. What is the average time the $4$ hamburgers spend on the shelf?
options: $2.25$ minutes
$9$ minutes
$5$ minutes
$4.75$ minutes

questions.question: Each day a restaurant prepares $4$ hamburgers at minute $0$, each sellable for $8$ minutes and then scrapped. On day 1 customers arrive at minutes $2$ and $5$; on day 2 at minutes $1,3,4,6,7$. What fraction of the $8$ hamburgers is scrapped?

The number of jobs $L(t)$ in a system on $[0,10)$ equals $0$ on $[0,1)$, $1$ on $[1,3)$, $0$ on $[3,4)$, $1$ on $[4,6)$, $2$ on $[6,7)$, $1$ on $[7,8)$ and $0$ on $[8,10)$. Let $Y(0,10)$ be the total time during $[0,10)$ in which no job is present. What is the estimate $Y(0,10)/10$ of $p(0)$, the fraction of time the system is empty?

Eight consecutive arriving patients each record the number of patients in the clinic just after they themselves have entered: $1,2,1,2,3,1,2,2$. What is the resulting estimate of $\pi(0)$, the fraction of arrivals that find the clinic empty?

Each day a restaurant prepares $S$ hamburgers; the customer arrival times on each day and the selling time are fixed. Which statement about raising $S$ by one hamburger, keeping everything else unchanged, is correct?
options: Both lost sales and scrapped hamburgers fall, because extra stock serves more customers.
Lost sales fall by exactly one on every day, because each day gains one hamburger.
Scrapped hamburgers stay the same, because an extra hamburger is always sold to someone.
Lost sales cannot increase and scrapped hamburgers cannot decrease on any of the days.

questions.question: A hospital department plans physician hours above its average daily consultation workload. Which effect is consistent with the trade-off between capacity and waiting in a queueing system?
options: Patients tend to wait less, and physicians are idle less, since the extra hours get used.
Patients tend to wait less, but physicians are idle for a larger fraction of their time.
Waiting does not change, since the average daily workload of the patients stays the same.
Idle time falls, since the extra hours absorb the urgent patients who would otherwise wait.

questions.question: For a system with $L(t)$ jobs at time $t$, which statement about how $p(n)$ and $\pi(n)$ weight the occurrences of state $n$ is correct?
options: $p(n)$ weights each visit to state $n$ by its duration, while $\pi(n)$ counts each arriving job once, by the state it finds.
$p(n)$ counts each visit to state $n$ once, while $\pi(n)$ weights each visit to state $n$ by its duration.
Both weight state $n$ by duration, but $\pi(n)$ uses only those periods in which the server is busy.
$p(n)$ weights state $n$ by its duration, while $\pi(n)$ counts each departing job by the state it leaves.

questions.question: A shop puts $2$ items on the shelf at minute $0$ and receives a new batch at minute $10$; items do not expire, and demand that finds an empty shelf is backlogged and served first from the new batch. Customers arrive at minutes $2$, $5$ and $7$, each wanting one item. Which pair gives the fraction of demand served from stock and the total time that customers spend waiting for an item?
options: $1/3$ served from stock, and a total wait of $3$ minutes
$2/3$ served from stock, and a total wait of $5$ minutes
$2/3$ served from stock, and a total wait of $3$ minutes
all demand served from stock, and a total wait of $3$ minutes

questions.question: A restaurant puts $3$ hamburgers on the shelf at minute $0$; each can be sold for $8$ minutes and is then scrapped. Three customers, each wanting one, arrive at minutes $2$, $5$ and $9$. Which pair gives the fraction of customers lost and the fraction of hamburgers scrapped?
options: $0$ lost and $0$ scrapped
$0$ lost and $1/3$ scrapped
$1/2$ lost and $1/3$ scrapped
$1/3$ lost and $1/3$ scrapped

questions.question: On half of the working days $8$ patients come and on the other half $12$, each needing $10$ minutes; physicians supply $100$ minutes every day, and work beyond that is done in overtime the same day. Which pair gives the average idle and overtime minutes per day?
options: $0$ idle and $0$ overtime
$20$ idle and $20$ overtime
$10$ idle and $0$ overtime
$10$ idle and $10$ overtime

questions.question: For a single-server queue it is known that $p(0)=0.1$, so the server is busy $90\%$ of the time. What can be concluded about the fraction of arriving jobs that find the server busy?
options: It must equal $0.9$, because long-run fractions of time and of arrivals coincide.
It must be at least $0.9$, because arrivals tend to occur while the server is busy.
It is not fixed by $p(0)$ alone, and with regular arrivals it can even be $0$.
It must be positive, because a server that is busy $90\%$ of the time is seen busy by some arrivals.

questions.question: Each day a restaurant prepares the same number $S$ of hamburgers, and all customers of a day arrive within the selling time; the daily customer counts $d_1,\ldots,d_m$ with $m\ge2$ are known. When does some $S$ give no lost sales and no scrap on every day?
options: Exactly when all daily counts $d_1,\ldots,d_m$ are equal; then $S$ is that common value.
Whenever $S$ is chosen equal to the average of the daily counts $d_1,\ldots,d_m$.
Whenever $S$ lies between the smallest and the largest of the daily counts $d_i$.
Whenever $S$ is chosen equal to the largest of the daily counts $d_1,\ldots,d_m$.

questions.question: Jobs arrive at a single server at times $0,1,10,11,20,21,\ldots$ (two per period of $10$) and are served in order of arrival, each taking $3$ time units. Which pair gives the long-run values of $p(0)$ and $\pi(0)$?

A restaurant must prepare the same number $S$ of hamburgers each day. Over three days $1$, $2$ and $5$ customers come within the selling time; a lost customer costs $2$ euro and a scrapped hamburger $2$ euro. Which $S$ minimises the total cost over the three days?
